title: Segmentation, targeting & positioning
source: Session 5 handout (DDM 26/27) – Lilien et al. (2017), Euromonitor Consumer Types, MyNatural case, Ries & Trout (2001), Levitt (1980)
tagline: Markets are heterogeneous. STP finds groups of similar customers (segmentation, with cluster analysis), decides which ones to serve (targeting, with the GE/McKinsey matrix) and builds a distinct place in their minds (positioning, with perceptual maps).
goals: explain the **STP** logic and how it creates value for the firm
explain how **cluster analysis** forms segments and how to test robustness
evaluate segment attractiveness and use the **GE/McKinsey matrix**
read a **perceptual map** and compare it with a brand association map

sections.heading: The STP approach
sections.lead: Customers differ in needs, wants, constraints, values, beliefs and incentives. STP identifies potential customers, selects which to pursue and formulates the value proposition for them.

blocks.title: How STP adds value (Lilien et al., 2017)

steps.label: Focus
steps.text: Resources focused to better meet needs and deliver more value

steps.label: Preference
steps.text: Customers prefer brands that meet their needs better

steps.label: Loyalty
steps.text: Repeat purchase, positive word of mouth

steps.label: Share & barrier
steps.text: Higher market share, barrier to competition

steps.label: Profit
steps.text: Fewer resources needed over time → profitability rises

blocks.title: Post-demographic segmentation
blocks.text: Traditional demographics (age, gender, income, family status, country) are **losing predictive power**. People construct lifestyles and identities of their own choosing – segment by needs, values, attitudes and behaviour.

items.text: A group of customers with similar needs and similar behaviour or lifestyle.

Identifying and grouping consumers into relatively **homogeneous** segments based on shared needs, characteristics, attitudes or behaviours – then evaluating and targeting them with tailored strategies.

sides.label: Short term
points: Today's competitors and my relative advantage

sides.label: Longer term
points: Emerging needs, new and evolving segments

points: Database review: primary and secondary data

blocks.title: Bases vs. descriptors – the model needs both

sides.label: Segmentation bases
sides.sub: Why segments differ → used to FORM the clusters
points: Variables on needs, attitudes, knowledge, uses, responses to the product
MyNatural: GreenValues, Knowledge, Evaluation, ProductBeliefs, Social

sides.label: Segment descriptors
sides.sub: Who they are → used to PROFILE and reach the clusters
points: Demographics, firmographics, personality, values, purchase frequency
MyNatural: age, gender, location, purchase frequency, willingness to try

blocks.note: The choice depends on the objective: tailoring campaigns to needs → psychographic or behavioural bases; expanding into new regions → geographic bases.

sections.heading: Cluster analysis
sections.lead: A statistical method that groups consumers on several variables so that people within a cluster are similar to each other and different from people in other clusters.

blocks.title: Shopping centre: four clusters on two dimensions
groups: Cluster 1 – largest: rare visits, moderately high spending
Cluster 4 – smallest: very frequent visits, moderately high spending
blocks.caption: The algorithm (e.g. k-means) minimises the average distance between customers **within** a cluster and maximises the distance **between** cluster centroids (×). Real segmentations use more than two variables.

blocks.title: Is the solution robust?
blocks.text: Randomly split the sample into two halves and re-run the analysis. The higher the agreement between the two solutions, the more robust the original cluster solution.

blocks.title: Example: Euromonitor “Voice of the Consumer: Lifestyles” consumer types

items.label: Cluster 1 – moderate greens
items.text: Average on all bases; medium purchase frequency and intentions. Volume segment – needs convincing on product benefits.

items.label: Cluster 2 – indifferent
items.text: Lowest green values, knowledge and social influence; rarely buys sustainable products; lowest purchase likelihood – despite the best evaluation of MyNatural.

items.label: Cluster 3 – green enthusiasts
items.text: Strongest values, knowledge, beliefs and peer influence; buys most often; highest willingness to try and recommend – but rates MyNatural **lowest**: improve product perception (healthy, sustainable, ethical).

blocks.text: “Positioning is not what you do to a product. Positioning is what you do to the **mind of a prospect**” (Ries & Trout). Firms should define themselves by the **value they produce in consumers' lives** – the value proposition (Levitt).

sides.label: Differentiation
points: Creating tangible or intangible differences on one or more attributes between your offering and competitors

sides.label: Positioning
points: Strategies to differentiate the offering **in the minds** of target customers
Success = a distinct, relevant and sustainable position

steps.text: Get ratings of competitors from a customer sample

blocks.title: Perceptual map (illustrative)
blocks.caption: Short distance = perceived as similar (A and B compete head-on). Axes = underlying dimensions consumers use to differentiate. Empty areas are potential positioning gaps – e.g. good value for money (C) faces little competition. Attribute vectors can be added.

blocks.title: Perceptual maps vs. brand association maps
head: Perceptual map
Brand association map
rows: How consumers perceive brands along key dimensions
The mental network of associations tied to a brand
No fixed axes – associations radiate around the brand
Easy to interpret, finds positioning gaps
Captures depth and richness of meaning

recap: STP: **segment** (identify) → **target** (select) → **position** (competitive advantage); value via focus, loyalty, share and profit.
Demographics lose predictive power → post-demographic segmentation by needs, values and behaviour.
**Bases** form the clusters (why they differ); **descriptors** profile and reach them (who they are).
Cluster analysis: small distance within clusters, large distance between centroids; robustness via split-half re-runs.
Attractiveness: size & growth, structural characteristics, product–market fit → GE/McKinsey matrix (attractiveness × strengths).
Positioning happens in the customer's mind; perceptual maps show similarity by distance and reveal gaps.
exam: Interpret a cluster table (means + profiling): name, size, attractiveness and an action per segment – the MyNatural pattern.
Bases vs. descriptors: classify given variables.
Place segments in the GE/McKinsey matrix and justify a strategy; read a perceptual map (who competes, where is a gap).
traps: The largest segment is not automatically the most attractive – fit and intentions matter (MyNatural cluster 3).
A high evaluation of the brand does not mean high purchase intention (cluster 2).
Differentiation is about the offering, positioning about the customer's perception.
